restatements.text: Authorizes a one-time tax on the personal property and wealth of California billionaires, establishes the permanently separate 2026 Billionaire Tax Reserve Fund, allocates 90% of its revenues to health care and 10% to education and food assistance, and exempts the revenues from standard state appropriation limits.

Directs the distribution of the Reserve Fund to Medi-Cal, K-14 education, and food programs like CalFresh, prohibits using the funds to replace existing state spending, requires the Department of Finance to report annually on the fund's status, and authorizes a $50 million start-up loan to the Franchise Tax Board.
Imposes a 5% excise tax for the 2026 tax year on the net worth of California residents and trusts with a net worth of $1 billion or more, and outlines reporting and payment options.

Establishes detailed valuation rules for various assets, requiring taxpayers to use a specific multiplier formula for private business interests, submit certified appraisals for assets over $1 million, and report the fair market value of items like art and vehicles, while exempting certain retirement accounts and directly held real property.

Grants the Franchise Tax Board authority to adopt regulations to enforce the tax, including identifying abusive transactions, and exempts these regulations from the Administrative Procedure Act until January 1, 2028.
Permits the Legislature to amend the Act with a two-thirds vote, provided the amendments further the measure's purposes.
Contains a severability clause ensuring that if any part of the Act is found invalid, the remaining provisions stay in effect.

Imposes penalties of 20% for substantial tax understatements and 40% for gross understatements, authorizes the Franchise Tax Board to disregard transactions lacking economic substance, and allows the Board to sue in superior court for a trial de novo if it disagrees with an Office of Tax Appeals decision.

Provides for an expedited validation action in Sacramento County Superior Court to determine the facial validity of the Act within 60 days of voter approval, with direct appeal to the California Supreme Court.
Prohibits taxpayers from deducting the state net worth tax from their state income taxes.

analysis.answer: Current law was not provided, but generally individuals are taxed on realized income rather than accumulated net worth. This measure changes current law by imposing a one-time 5% excise tax on the total net worth of California residents (and applicable trusts) whose wealth exceeds $1 billion.

Direct costs include administrative expenses for the Franchise Tax Board, which is authorized to receive a $50 million start-up loan. Taxpayers will face substantial compliance costs to obtain certified appraisals for complex assets like private businesses and art. There may also be broader economic opportunity costs if wealthy residents relocate or move capital out of the state to avoid the tax.

California residents with a net worth over $1 billion will pay the tax. The intended beneficiaries are low- and moderate-income individuals receiving health coverage through Medi-Cal, as well as students and families relying on public education and food assistance programs.

Affected individuals will likely employ complex financial and legal strategies to avoid the tax, such as relocating to other states before the tax obligation date, transferring assets to trusts, or contesting the constitutionality of the measure in court. The Franchise Tax Board will need to hire outside experts and establish complex new valuation methodologies.

The measure addresses projected state budget shortfalls and federal funding cuts for safety-net programs by taxing the state's wealthiest individuals. While the mechanism—a one-time 5% wealth tax—is designed to raise significant revenue, its effectiveness may be limited by capital flight, avoidance strategies, and the difficulty of accurately appraising privately held, illiquid assets.
The Franchise Tax Board gains significant new discretion and power to write rules exempt from the Administrative Procedure Act until 2028, audit returns, and challenge appeal decisions in court.

Researchers disagree on whether state-level wealth taxes raise substantial, lasting revenue. Some research suggests such taxes can successfully capture revenue with minimal behavioral changes, while other findings indicate they lead to significant out-migration of wealthy residents and capital flight, ultimately reducing long-term tax revenues.

Significant resources will be lost to administration and enforcement, as the state and taxpayers will need to hire experts, appraisers, and outside counsel to determine the value of closely held businesses, complex trusts, and private assets, likely resulting in prolonged litigation.
The measure can be amended by a two-thirds vote of the Legislature, but only if the amendments are consistent with and further the purposes of the Act.

flags.quote: To the extent any provision of Article XIIIA would otherwise be construed to limit, restrict, or apply to the rate, base, valuation, or imposition of the tax authorized by this Section, that provision shall not apply to, and is superseded by, this Section.
flags.note: Overrides other constitutional limits on taxes and property valuation.

flags.quote: (a) The provisions of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, also referred to as "the Act," are severable.

The Legislature may amend the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, by statute passed in each house of the Legislature by rollcall vote entered in the journal, two-thirds of the membership concurring, ifthe statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.
flags.note: Requires a supermajority and limits amendments to those furthering the measure's purposes.
